## CodeGraph

In repositories indexed by CodeGraph (a `.codegraph/` directory exists at the repo root), reach for it BEFORE grep/find or reading files when you need to understand or locate code:

- **MCP tool** (when available): `codegraph_explore` answers most code questions in one call — the relevant symbols' verbatim source plus the call paths between them, including dynamic-dispatch hops grep can't follow. Name a file or symbol in the query to read its current line-numbered source. If it's listed but deferred, load it by name via tool search.
- **Shell** (always works): `codegraph explore "<symbol names or question>"` prints the same output.

If there is no `.codegraph/` directory, skip CodeGraph entirely — indexing is the user's decision.
<!-- CODEGRAPH_END -->

<!-- ENGLISH_PILOT_GUIDANCE_START -->
## EnglishPilot

Do not derail the main task. When the user prompt is allowed, complete the requested work first.
If the prompt contains any Chinese fragment, awkward English, or an obvious everyday phrasing improvement, add one English note at the end of the final response when allowed and teachable.
In force/high intensity, treat this as required unless there is genuinely no useful improvement.

When the english-pilot MCP server is available, use `english_coaching_context` to get the configured note depth and response guidance before writing the final answer.
Use `english_rewrite_text` and `english_pronounce_text` for structured help when useful.

If MCP is unavailable, prefer this fallback format:
Use a Rich English Note by default: 5-8 useful lines, brief enough for a final response but rich enough for study.
Use this shape:
English note:
Original: "fix this problem"
Better: "fix this issue" / "resolve this startup issue"
Why: In engineering conversations, "issue" is more precise than "problem" when discussing bugs, failures, tickets, or startup errors.
Useful patterns:
- "The MCP client failed during the startup handshake."
- "This issue belongs at the config boundary, not the runtime path."
Collocations: startup issue, handshake failure, config mismatch, reproduce the issue, verify the fix
Common mistake: Use "problem" for general trouble; use "issue" for bugs, tickets, incidents, and engineering discussions.
IPA: issue /ˈɪʃuː/ or /ˈɪsjuː/

When the user asks for a recap, lesson, speech, or review based on their history, use `english_learning_brief`, `english_input_history`, or `english_notes_history` before answering.
Do not add an English note for prompts blocked by the EnglishPilot hook.
<!-- ENGLISH_PILOT_GUIDANCE_END -->

# Repository Guidelines

## Roadmap and task execution

- Read the [development roadmap](docs/development-roadmap.md) before selecting
  planned work. It owns the thirty-source consolidation, foundation scope,
  priorities, task dependencies, phase acceptance, current claims and deferred
  features; this file owns the execution rules. Existing guides retain authority
  over product/security/resource contracts.
- The planning change must merge through the existing PR/review/current-head
  checks before product execution. Start the execution cycle from that accepted
  `main` revision, beginning with F01, then select tasks with accepted relevant
  inputs. A planning merge or an existing test file is not implementation or
  acceptance evidence. Do not bypass gates or resume an unmerged planning
  snapshot as though it were the accepted baseline.
- Deliver the finite current-IM foundations and their integrated acceptance
  before post-foundation features. Forum, PWA, marketplace, external SDK and other
  roadmap-only directions require a recorded activation decision; do not build
  their speculative infrastructure during foundation work. Verified urgent
  security, data-loss or hard-freeze findings override ordinary order.
- Before a claim, recheck the live tracker, existing branches/PRs and ownership.
  Register one task owner, source/parent SHA, outcome, exact owned paths, accepted
  inputs, shared-interface/integration owner, evidence and next action. Reuse
  existing work without silently reassigning it. Keep one authoritative live
  claim record and update state/evidence before releasing the claim.
- Admit parallel mutations only with stable accepted inputs/interfaces,
  independent path and policy ownership, a clear integration order and available
  review/validation capacity. Do not start work expected to need reimplementation
  when an upstream change merges. Separate files do not prove independence;
  serialize uncertain shared contracts or limit preparation to read-only work.
  Stop and reassess dependents when their accepted interface changes.
- For coordinated parallel tasks, declare an integration branch, create children
  from its accepted tip/parent, and merge reviewed, validated compatible results
  back in dependency order before integrated acceptance and the main PR gates.
  Preserve the [worktree lifecycle](#worktree-lifecycle); never sweep unrelated
  changes or bypass preservation/cleanup rules.
- Treat module extraction as a bounded change with a real existing consumer,
  explicit policy/lifecycle/errors and recovery evidence. Measure selected
  performance paths before and after; deliver regression protection and maintained
  decisions with each slice. Retain working boundaries when no justified change
  is needed. Unknown facts become bounded investigations, not assumed defects,
  numerical targets, migrations or commitments to future features.

## Reliability before implementation

- For background work, synchronization, storage, caching or UI-state changes, read
  [performance requirements](docs/performance-requirements.md). Identify the work
  trigger, resource budget, accumulation/reclamation policy and applicable
  performance regression before editing; record measured limits and remaining
  gaps. Apply its [startup, idle and active-business checklist](docs/performance-requirements.md#apply-to-every-feature)
  to every affected phase, including return to idle after use. Extend its general
  rules when a confirmed defect reveals a new pattern.

- Before implementing, refactoring, fixing or reviewing code, read the
  [AI coding reliability guide](docs/ai-coding-reliability.md), select the rules
  triggered by the changed boundaries, and inspect the owning code and callers.
  For concurrency/lifecycle changes, trace lock order, wait dependencies, actual
  work ownership, cancellation and commit authority before editing.
- Validate the applicable failure and recovery paths, not only the happy path.
  Record concrete evidence and remaining limits; a timeout, successful build or
  passing subset is not proof that UI freezes or all deadlocks are impossible.
- When a confirmed defect exposes a reusable failure pattern, update that guide's
  existing rule or add a distinct rule with its owner and regression evidence.
  Maintain the owning contract and test selectors; keep incident logs out of the guide.

## Project Structure & Module Organization

- Four-crate Rust workspace. `crates/mesh-talk-core/` is the UI-free protocol core (lib
  `mesh_talk_core` + the `mesh-talk-node` CLI bin in `src/bin/`): feature modules `node/`,
  `identity/`, `transport/`, `discovery/`, `eventlog/`, `ratchet/`, `channel/`, `dm.rs`,
  `file/`, `postoffice/`, `storage/`. `src-tauri/` is the Tauri desktop app: entry
  `src/main.rs` → `lib.rs`, IPC glue in `commands.rs` (auth) + `chat_commands/` (messaging)
  - `events.rs`, plus `state.rs`, `tray.rs`, `services/` (auth only).
- `crates/mesh-talk-integrations/` owns scoped local messaging grants, private IPC,
  and the dedicated bot host/admin CLI; `crates/mesh-talk-mcp/` adapts its four
  send/context/status tools to the official MCP SDK. Neither owns mesh crypto.
- Integration/e2e suites live in `crates/mesh-talk-core/tests/` (`two_node_cli`,
  `persistent_history`, `post_office_offline`, `decoder_smoke`); keep unit tests inline via
  `mod tests` (e.g. `node/node_tests.rs`).
- React client sits in `frontend/src`; Vite tooling in `frontend/package.json`.
- Operational scripts in `scripts/` (`setup-hooks.sh`, `check-health.sh`); architecture in
  `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`; conventions in `specifications/`. The
  [documentation map](docs/README.md) routes readers to maintained guides; the
  [documentation guidelines](docs/DOCUMENTATION_GUIDELINES.md) define ownership
  across the README, guides, and project site.

## Build, Test, and Development Commands

- `make dev` primes Rust + Node deps and installs git hooks.
- `make build` / `make frontend-build` — release build / Vite production build.
- During feature development, preview changed-boundary validation with `make test-plan`
  and run it with `make test-changed`. Unmapped changes require an explicit owner
  and reason; inspect escalation notes for browser/native or consumer checks.
  Use `make verify-plan` / `make verify-changed` at task completion to compose the
  same affected tests with applicable formatting, lint/types and builds. The
  test-only commands do not include static checks; neither mode replaces required
  PR/review, browser/native or release gates. `make validation-report` separates
  queue and execution costs; `make validation-audit` compares a clean affected
  plan with same-source broader failure evidence before narrowing any gate.
  Read selected capability references and inspect pending browser/native requirements.
  Execution prints a structured feedback report; follow the
  [validation protocol](docs/testing-feedback-loop.md#validation-stages-and-agent-responsibilities)
  for completed work, remaining evidence and additive semantic selections.
- During feature development, run affected tests only: `make test-focused
TEST_PACKAGE=mesh-talk-core TEST_FILTER=node::account_sync` selects Rust unit
  tests; add `TEST_TARGET=bridge_cross_lan` to select one integration target.
  `cd frontend && npm test -- src/features/chat/settingsDialogSession.test.ts`
  selects a frontend unit file. `make test` runs the full workspace suite
  (`cargo test --workspace`) for pre-PR and CI gates;
  `make e2e` runs the `#[ignore]`d multi-process backend rigs; `cd frontend && npm run e2e`
  runs the Playwright UI suite. Test builds use cheap KDF params (the `fast-test-kdf`
  feature), and `.cargo/config.toml` caps test/compile parallelism.
- UI / node spot checks: `make tauri-dev`, `make frontend-dev`,
  `cargo run -p mesh-talk-core --bin mesh-talk-node -- --keystore /tmp/a.keystore
--password pw --name alice` (add `--post-office` for relay mode).

## Coding Style & Naming Conventions

- Rust: `cargo fmt` (4-space, `snake_case` modules, `UpperCamelCase` types) +
  **`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`** (must match CI — `--all-targets` covers
  tests/benches).
- Frontend: `npm run format` (Prettier) + `npm run lint` (ESLint flat config).
- Write documentation and reusable prompts in English unless a specific exception is needed.
- Reference `specifications/development_conventions.md` for naming nuances.

## Domain Language

- `CONTEXT.md` is the canonical domain glossary. `docs/domain-design.md` indexes
  the modeling references and defines DDD vocabulary and naming translations.
- Distinguish local users, accounts and devices; desktop, transport and ratchet
  sessions; discovery, presence, custody, recipient delivery and read state.
- Use explicit identity/lifetime names in new code. Preserve public, wire and
  stored identifiers unless a separately validated compatibility change is intended.
- Update the glossary and affected owning guides when a domain meaning changes;
  link to definitions instead of maintaining duplicate glossaries.

## Architecture & Components

- Before adding business logic, consult [module ownership and reuse](docs/module-boundaries.md),
  inspect the owning module and its callers, and extend its existing implementation.
  Parallel tasks should name their owned paths and shared-interface dependencies;
  coordinate changes to shared interfaces through one integration owner. Keep
  feature-specific helpers local and share rules when their meaning and lifecycle
  are the same. The guide owns the detailed assignment and handoff contract.
- Stack: Rust 2024 on Tokio; Tauri 2 + React shell. No vendor-operated server.
- The `Node` (`node/node.rs`) wires identity + signed UDP **multicast** discovery
  (group `224.0.0.167`, port 47474) + Noise-encrypted TCP transport (`transport/`,
  low-level socket in `transport/net.rs`) + the content-addressed event log + DM/channel/
  file crypto. Messages are events synced as a bounded append-only log, account-addressed
  across a user's devices; optional offline custody via equal eligible post offices.
  Routed discovery and opt-in post-office federation connect reachable sites without
  joining their IP subnets. Wire formats are versioned bincode.
- See **`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`** before changing crypto, sync, or transport;
  **`docs/network-design-reference.md`** owns the communication invariants,
  module contracts, resource budgets and topology acceptance boundaries.

## Maintaining standards as requirements change

- Before changing tests, fixtures, dependencies or workflows in ways that affect
  CI cost or reliability, read [CI maintenance](docs/ci-maintenance.md). Reuse
  existing owners, measure the affected cost, and preserve acceptance evidence;
  keep required-check policy in its existing owner.
- Before implementation, identify the existing decision owner, authoritative rule,
  observable acceptance criteria, affected consumers and required boundary evidence.
  Extend the owning implementation and `validation.json`; new business capabilities
  should link their guide and invariants. Explain an unchanged contract in the PR.
- Run `make standards-check` after adding/moving source or changing contracts. It
  checks structural ownership and maintained references, including new files; it
  does not prove assertion quality, semantic completeness or candidate readiness.
  Hooks inspect the working tree, so partially staged commits still need a clean
  committed-candidate check in CI. Frontend dependencies must be installed.
- When CI exposes a local omission or flaky fixture, fix the owning selector, task
  or fixture and add a focused regression. Review timing and selection evidence
  before changing policy. Follow the maintained
  [requirement maintenance loop](docs/testing-feedback-loop.md#maintaining-standards-across-requirements).

## Testing Guidelines

- Integration coverage in `crates/mesh-talk-core/tests/` and `node/node_tests.rs`; embed
  unit tests near the code. Networking/crypto changes ship a loopback integration assertion.
- Backend multi-process E2E via `make e2e` (CI: `e2e-backend.yml`); Playwright UI E2E via
  `cd frontend && npm run e2e` (CI: `e2e-ui.yml`).
- Do not run full suites or E2E automatically during ordinary feature work. Run
  the affected unit or integration tests as changes are made; run E2E and the
  comprehensive health gate on explicit request, for optional full local preparation,
  or in CI.
- See `docs/testing-feedback-loop.md` for selection examples and escalation triggers.
- Document executed validation commands in every PR; ensure `make test` passes
  locally or through its matching CI workspace suite before merge.

## Commit & Pull Request Guidelines

- Before changing product versions or release automation, read [the version lifecycle](docs/updates.md#version-ownership-and-lifecycle).
  Root `Cargo.toml` `[workspace.package].version` is authoritative. Use
  `node scripts/release/version.mjs check|sync|prepare VERSION` (the `VERSION` argument belongs
  to `prepare` only); do not hand-edit generated npm/Cargo lock metadata or introduce another
  version constant. Root private npm metadata is a checked release-tooling projection;
  frontend private metadata is versionless and Tauri inherits Cargo. Never broadly replace
  matching dependency, fixture, history, wire or schema versions. Keep source builds `BASE-dev`,
  Nightlies `BASE-nightly.RUN.ATTEMPT`, official tagged builds `BASE`, and standard SemVer ordering.
- Version/changelog preparation and next-development-target changes use reviewed PRs. Ordinary main
  pushes must not create automatic release proposals or commit-derived product notes. Stable publication
  remains explicit through the existing verified tagged-release workflow; no direct main push,
  public empty release, mutable published tag or gate bypass. Nightly publication requires trusted
  `main` and a target above the latest Stable. Future changes must extend the existing version
  owner, its tests, standards/CI enforcement and capability contracts together; the owning guide
  documents permissions, bot-PR checks, dispatch and recovery requirements. Manual Stable draft
  preparation uses the reviewed exact-version CHANGELOG section and requires exact-source checks
  before creating its immutable tag/draft. The fixed release-history
  migration floor is historical provenance; never advance it during ordinary version bumps.

- Conventional commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`); scopes like `feat(node):` align with
  `specifications/git_standards.md`. Squash WIP; link issues. When asked to merge,
  default to squash merge unless the user explicitly requests another strategy;
  follow the [merge policy](specifications/git_standards.md#pull-request-merge-strategy)
  and current-head required checks.
- Create PRs through `./scripts/create-pr.sh -- <gh pr create options>`.
  The default checks the clean committed candidate, comparison base, argument safety,
  whitespace, cheap affected static checks, ownership blockers, structural standards,
  repository hygiene and applicable verified frontend patch coverage before publication.
  Use `make pr-check` for the same cheap static phase; missing current coverage
  evidence reports its explicit generation command and never starts suites implicitly.
  CI runs after publication; full-scope candidates retain cross-platform execution.
  Only the proven [documentation scope](docs/ci-maintenance.md#documentation-only-pr-scope)
  may omit unrelated product tests. All required checks must pass on the current PR head before merging. Creating a PR does not certify test acceptance.
- To run comprehensive checks locally before publication, use
  `./scripts/create-pr.sh --full-preflight <selectors/specs> -- <gh pr create options>`.
  This invokes `prepare-pr.sh` (platform preflight plus full health). For an existing
  PR, `./scripts/prepare-pr.sh <selectors/specs>` provides the same optional local gate.
  Use Playwright specs relevant to changed frontend behavior and repeated
  `--core-filter` / `--host-filter` / `--integration-filter` / `--mcp-filter` selectors
  for changed Rust crates. Preflight runs selected tests in Linux Docker and through
  SSH to `windows10`; Windows workspaces, caches and temporary data stay on drive D.
  Owning scenario rules add visual specs and require real native evidence for
  lifecycle/discovery changes. Missing environments or empty Rust selections fail
  full preflight. Include `e2e/ui-visual-regression.spec.ts` for theme/layout changes.
  See `docs/testing-feedback-loop.md` for configuration, coverage and plan preview.
  Fetch `origin/main` first if the comparison base is stale.
- Record focused validation and outstanding checks in the PR. Use
  `./scripts/check-health.sh` when comprehensive local evidence is needed; protected
  CI remains required before merge regardless of local results.

## Security & Adjustments

- `./scripts/check-health.sh` chains fmt, Clippy `--all-targets`, ESLint, tests, typos,
  cargo-deny, cargo-machete, gitleaks, shellcheck, audits, and both builds.
- Triage vulnerabilities immediately or document mitigation in the PR.
- If plans shift, update the relevant committed design or architecture docs. Keep
  `docs/superpowers/` and the root `plans/` directory local and untracked.

## Repository Hygiene

### Worktree lifecycle

- Create a worktree only when isolation is needed. Before creating one, inspect
  `git worktree list --porcelain` and record the task-owned path, branch and any
  dedicated build directory in ignored `tmp/` task notes. Treat pre-existing
  worktrees and unrelated changes as user-owned; never sweep them automatically.
- The coordinating session owns cleanup of every worktree it creates or delegates,
  including `.worktrees/` and `.claude/worktrees/agent-*`. Delegate completion does
  not transfer that responsibility. Before ending the task, stop task-owned
  processes and remove its worktrees, disposable branches and dedicated Cargo
  target directories, subject to the preservation rules below. Never delete a
  shared target directory or a directory whose ownership is uncertain.
- Before removal, preserve the work through either a verified merge into the
  intended integration branch under the existing PR/merge gates, or a local
  archive. For an archive, commit only task-owned outstanding changes (including
  intended untracked files), run the required commit checks, and create a unique
  `archive/<worktree-name>-<timestamp>` tag at the final branch tip. Verify the tag
  resolves to that tip and the worktree is clean before deleting anything. Never
  overwrite an existing archive tag, include secrets/ignored build output, or
  discard unrelated edits to make cleanup succeed. Cleanup does not authorize
  merging, pushing, bypassing review or running `entire clean`.
- Run removal from a surviving checkout with `git worktree remove <path>`, then
  `git branch -d <branch>` for a merged branch. Use `git branch -D <branch>` only
  for a task-owned archived branch after verifying its archive tag. Never use
  forced worktree removal, hard reset or bulk directory deletion to bypass a
  dirty worktree. Detached worktrees require the same preservation of their final
  commit before removal; there is no branch to delete.
- A pending PR, unresolved conflict, user decision, active concurrent session or
  failed preservation/cleanup step is an explicit retention exception. Preserve
  the required branch for an open PR; remove its clean worktree if no active work
  needs it. Recheck `git worktree list --porcelain` and task-owned branches/build
  paths before the final reply. Report cleanup performed and name every retained
  path/branch, its reason and the next action; never silently leave task worktrees.

- Keep implementation plans, research, investigation notes and scratch scripts
  under ignored `tmp/`; remove them when the work is complete.
- Merge durable decisions into the maintained owning guide. Do not commit
  completed-work reports, score histories, duplicate runbooks or archive copies.
- `docs/evals/` owns reusable suites/inventories, prompts and its README only.
  Generated evidence belongs in ignored output or PR/CI artifacts.
- Run `node scripts/check-repository-hygiene.mjs` before committing. The shared
  index check also runs in pre-commit, CI and health, rejecting ignored files
  even when force-added. See `docs/DOCUMENTATION_GUIDELINES.md` for ownership.

# Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

In Default mode, strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing the user's request rather than stopping to ask questions.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.

If explicit user input is required for another reason before progress can safely continue, do not use the `request_user_input` tool. Ask the user directly with one concise plain-text question instead. Never write a multiple choice question as a textual assistant message.

## Instruction Priority

Superpowers skills override default system prompt behavior, but **user instructions always take precedence**:

1. **User's explicit instructions** (CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md, direct requests) — highest priority
2. **Superpowers skills** — override default system behavior where they conflict
3. **Default system prompt** — lowest priority

If CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, or AGENTS.md says "don't use TDD" and a skill says "always use TDD," follow the user's instructions. The user is in control.

## How to Access Skills

**In Claude Code:** Use the `Skill` tool. When you invoke a skill, its content is loaded and presented to you—follow it directly. Never use the Read tool on skill files.

**In Gemini CLI:** Skills activate via the `activate_skill` tool. Gemini loads skill metadata at session start and activates the full content on demand.

**In other environments:** Check your platform's documentation for how skills are loaded.

## Platform Adaptation

Skills use Claude Code tool names. Non-CC platforms: see `references/codex-tools.md` (Codex) for tool equivalents. Gemini CLI users get the tool mapping loaded automatically via GEMINI.md.

# Using Skills

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action.** Even a 1% chance a skill might apply means that you should invoke the skill to check. If an invoked skill turns out to be wrong for the situation, you don't need to use it.

```dot

    "User message received" [shape=doublecircle];
    "About to EnterPlanMode?" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Already brainstormed?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke brainstorming skill" [shape=box];
    "Might any skill apply?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke Skill tool" [shape=box];
    "Announce: 'Using [skill] to [purpose]'" [shape=box];
    "Has checklist?" [shape=diamond];
    "Create TodoWrite todo per item" [shape=box];
    "Follow skill exactly" [shape=box];
    "Respond (including clarifications)" [shape=doublecircle];

    "About to EnterPlanMode?" -> "Already brainstormed?";
    "Already brainstormed?" -> "Invoke brainstorming skill" [label="no"];
    "Already brainstormed?" -> "Might any skill apply?" [label="yes"];
    "Invoke brainstorming skill" -> "Might any skill apply?";

    "User message received" -> "Might any skill apply?";

    "Might any skill apply?" -> "Respond (including clarifications)" [label="definitely not"];

```

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

## Skill Priority

# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Git worktrees create isolated workspaces sharing the same repository, allowing work on multiple branches simultaneously without switching.

**Core principle:** Systematic directory selection + safety verification = reliable isolation.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."

## Directory Selection Process

Follow this priority order:

### 1. Check Existing Directories

```bash
# Check in priority order
ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
```

**If found:** Use that directory. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

### 2. Check CLAUDE.md


# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Git worktrees create isolated workspaces sharing the same repository, allowing work on multiple branches simultaneously without switching.

**Core principle:** Systematic directory selection + safety verification = reliable isolation.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."

## Directory Selection Process

Follow this priority order:

### 1. Check Existing Directories

```bash
# Check in priority order
ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
```

**If found:** Use that directory. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

### 2. Check CLAUDE.md

```bash
grep -i "worktree.*director" CLAUDE.md 2>/dev/null
```

**If preference specified:** Use it without asking.

### 3. Ask User

If no directory exists and no CLAUDE.md preference:

```
No worktree directory found. Where should I create worktrees?

1. .worktrees/ (project-local, hidden)
2. ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/<project-name>/ (global location)

Which would you prefer?
```

### For Project-Local Directories (.worktrees or worktrees)

**MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**

```bash
# Check if directory is ignored (respects local, global, and system gitignore)
git check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null
```

**If NOT ignored:**

Per Jesse's rule "Fix broken things immediately":
1. Add appropriate line to .gitignore
2. Commit the change
3. Proceed with worktree creation

**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.

### For Global Directory (~/.config/superpowers/worktrees)

No .gitignore verification needed - outside project entirely.

## Creation Steps

### 1. Detect Project Name

```bash
project=$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")
```

### 2. Create Worktree

```bash
# Determine full path
case $LOCATION in
  .worktrees|worktrees)
    path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
  ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/*)
    path="~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/$project/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
esac

# Create worktree with new branch
git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
cd "$path"
```

### 3. Run Project Setup

Auto-detect and run appropriate setup:

```bash

if [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi

# Rust
if [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi

# Python
if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi

# Go
if [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi
```

### 4. Verify Clean Baseline

Run tests to ensure worktree starts clean:

```bash
# Examples - use project-appropriate command
npm test
cargo test
pytest
go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.

**If tests pass:** Report ready.

### 5. Report Location

```

Tests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement <feature-name>
```

| `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |

| Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |

## Common Mistakes

### Skipping ignore verification

### Assuming directory location

- **Problem:** Creates inconsistency, violates project conventions

# AI coding reliability guide

Use this guide before implementing or reviewing a change, especially a bug fix,
refactor, merge resolution or optimization. Its purpose is to turn recurring
failure modes into concrete design questions and executable checks. Compiling,
adding a timeout or passing a happy-path test does not establish reliability.

This guide owns the cross-cutting review method and reusable failure patterns.
[Module ownership](module-boundaries.md) owns implementation boundaries;
[architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md), [network contracts](network-design-reference.md)
and feature guides own behavior and resource limits. The
[testing workflow](testing-feedback-loop.md) owns commands, selection and gates.
Link to those owners instead of copying their changing contracts here. When code
and a contract disagree, resolve the intended behavior rather than documenting
the regression as the new rule.

## Use on every change

1. **Locate the owner and consumers.** Read the owning implementation, callers,
   existing tests and relevant guide before adding another helper or state owner.
   Include callbacks, IPC handlers, retries, startup, shutdown and recovery paths;
   an import graph alone cannot reveal all consumers.
2. **State the invariant and select risks.** Describe what must remain true on
   success, failure, cancellation and replacement. Use the table below to select
   applicable rules. A small diff can change lock order or lifetime semantics.
3. **Trace the failure path before editing.** For concurrency work, sketch who
   owns each lock, permit, task and mutable state; what it waits for; and who
   releases it. For a reproducible bug, construct a focused failing regression.
   Record unresolved hypotheses as hypotheses, not confirmed defects.
4. **Implement at the existing boundary.** Preserve authority, durable acceptance,
   compatibility and resource budgets. Recheck invariants after moving work
   outside a guard. Evaluate the proposed fix for new races and deadlocks too.
5. **Verify the changed boundary and report evidence.** Run affected checks and
   required boundary scenarios under the testing workflow. Explain results,
   exclusions and unresolved evidence. Update this guide when the defect exposes
   a reusable failure pattern; follow the maintenance procedure below.

Accessible message summaries are consumer contracts. When photo, expression or
file naming changes, update browser selectors and the owning `prScenarios`
selection together; retain payload, privacy and receipt assertions instead of
restoring implementation-specific names for tests. The inline-media owner uses
`screenshot-portable.spec.ts` and `automatic-delivery.spec.ts` to cover screenshot
sending and group custody alongside the presentation scenarios.

Keep the risk explanation proportional to the change. A documentation edit does
not require a new concurrency test. A changed async callback does require a
lifetime review even when the diff is one line. Put task-specific reasoning and
results in the PR or ignored local evidence, not a new permanent report.

Cross-cutting idle budgets, demand-driven work and accumulation rules belong to
[performance requirements](performance-requirements.md). Apply them alongside the
correctness rules below; a smaller resource chart does not prove preserved recovery.

## Select rules by the changed boundary

| Change or symptom                                                        | Read at least                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Locks, callbacks, synchronous dispatch, UI freezes                       | [R01](#r01-lock-order-and-reentrant-calls), [R02](#r02-thread-and-scheduler-progress), [R10](#r10-evidence-that-exercises-the-failure)                |
| Background work, native providers, logout, shutdown or cancellation      | [R02](#r02-thread-and-scheduler-progress), [R03](#r03-actual-work-owns-its-lifetime), [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions)               |
| Network requests, retries, polling, queues or batches                    | [R03](#r03-actual-work-owns-its-lifetime), [R04](#r04-deadlines-cover-the-whole-operation), [R05](#r05-bounded-work-must-also-make-progress)          |
| React effects, IPC reads, dialogs, optimistic updates or mutation status | [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions), [R07](#r07-observation-is-not-mutation-ownership), [R10](#r10-evidence-that-exercises-the-failure) |
| Storage, settings, imports, deletion or recovery                         | [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions), [R08](#r08-durable-state-and-failure-semantics), [R09](#r09-bound-input-and-resource-use)          |
| IPC/API inputs, files, media or protocol changes                         | [R06](#r06-exact-authority-and-stale-completions), [R08](#r08-durable-state-and-failure-semantics), [R09](#r09-bound-input-and-resource-use)          |
| Merge resolution, shared helper or dependency changes                    | Revisit the affected callers and all applicable rules; a clean textual merge does not establish compatible ownership or semantics.                    |

# Module Ownership and Reuse

This is the implementation ownership map for maintaining Mesh Talk and assigning
parallel work. Use it to locate the owner of a decision before adding another
implementation. Network semantics and configuration belong to the
[communication architecture](network-design-reference.md); this document defines
where those decisions live in code and how to change them safely.

The [canonical glossary](../CONTEXT.md) defines domain concepts;
[DDD conventions](domain-design.md) define modeling terms and identifier mappings.
The layers and owners below are implementation responsibilities, not declarations
that every module or crate is a separate DDD bounded context.

## 1. Dependency direction

| Layer                                       | Owns                                                                                          | Depends on                                              | Must delegate                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Protocol core: `crates/mesh-talk-core`      | Identity, membership, encryption, admission, persistence, transport and delivery correctness  | Rust libraries and its internal modules                 | Native platform behavior and presentation                            |
| Desktop host: `src-tauri`                   | Session/runtime installation, OS integration, settings persistence, authorized IPC adaptation | Core public exports                                     | Wire validation, cryptographic authority and delivery state machines |
| Typed IPC: `frontend/src/lib/api`           | Command names, payload shapes, typed results                                                  | Shared types, Tauri APIs and sibling adapters           | UI stores, React features and business decisions                     |
| Application stores: `frontend/src/store`    | Reactive state, owner-scoped work, optimistic intents, cache transitions                      | Typed adapters and shared projections                   | Core authority and feature rendering                                 |
| Feature modules: `frontend/src/features`    | User interaction and composition                                                              | Stores, typed adapters, shared models and UI primitives | Reimplementation of identity, policy or delivery rules               |
| UI primitives: `frontend/src/components/ui` | Accessible visual controls                                                                    | React/Radix and styling helpers                         | Session lifecycle and protocol policy                                |

The bot integration service in `crates/mesh-talk-integrations` depends on the core
and host-supplied admission ports. It owns grants, bounded metadata audit and
private IPC and its fixed-route loopback HTTP adapter; `crates/mesh-talk-mcp` owns SDK/stdio translation only. Core
`node/outgoing_message.rs` owns retry-safe event acceptance and sender-state WAL
recovery. Desktop `src-tauri/src/integrations.rs` binds exact-session leases and
graceful listener retirement. `integrations/local_access.rs` owns serialized
settings/startup control and the single desktop service handle;
`integrations/instructions.rs` owns only the marked user-level bootstrap file.
Both transports share one integration service/registry and core sending path.
`http.rs` owns public static discovery, request limits and fixed scoped routes;
request schemas derive from the existing models. The Agent access settings UI uses
the shared save coordinator and an explicit-owner typed adapter. See
[desktop local access](bot-integrations.md#desktop-local-agent-access).

The local access owner persists absolute authorization deadlines and preserves
them across service retries and session/runtime restarts. Only an explicitly
verified enable, duration extension or renewal can extend authority. The shared
integration grant authorizer checks expiry again at core acceptance. The desktop
activity view uses the existing registry's bounded content-free send projection:
read the live service registry while its supervisor exists, and open the saved
registry only after its writer has stopped under the same controller serialization.
The UI never creates a second grant-store owner or attributes a shared credential
to a particular AI application. See [authorization lifetime](bot-integrations.md#lifecycle-and-authority).

The headless CLI uses the core directly. A protocol change should not require
Tauri; a presentation change should not alter the wire protocol. Not every helper
in `lib/` is pure: `theme.ts`, for example, owns reactive appearance effects. Use
specific modules rather than assuming the directory name implies purity.

The existing API facade remains stable. Its settings owner resolver is composed
at the application seam; adapters never import stores. ESLint enforces that rule
for alias imports and relative imports at any nesting depth. The auth store uses
low-level adapters to avoid recreating the facade/settings/auth runtime cycle.

ESLint also rejects static imports of rendering modules (`components/` and
`features/`) from stores and IPC adapters, including type-only imports and nested
relative paths. Shared presence vocabulary lives in `lib/presence.ts`; identity
controls re-export it for compatibility. Stores own evidence expiry and state
transitions; controls own visual mapping. These checks cover direct static
dependencies, not transitive dependencies or dynamic imports.

## 2. Feature owners and shared decisions

Paths below are relative to the repository root. `core/` abbreviates

# Implementation status and acceptance boundaries

This stable path is the current status index, not a chronological TODO list or a
claim that every topology/platform combination has been verified. Feature and
protocol details belong to the linked owning guides; Git history records completed
work.

## Current capability areas

| Area                       | Implemented behavior                                                                                                                             | Reference / boundary                                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Direct conversations       | Signed discovery, identity-pinned Noise/TCP, encrypted account-addressed DMs, replies, reactions, mentions, search and retained history.         | [Architecture](../docs/ARCHITECTURE.md); discovery and TCP reachability remain separate.                                                                                                |
| Groups                     | Signed membership controls, sender-key encryption, bounded fanout and authorized member recovery with per-member sharing.                        | [Group flows and scenarios](../docs/network-design-reference.md#d-group-creation-distribution-and-member-recovery); a removed/nonmember device cannot acquire authority from discovery. |
| Relay networking           | Equal trusted post offices, shared public enrollment, opaque custody/federation, direct-first attempts, soft preference and alternatives.        | [Network baseline](../docs/network-design-reference.md); an alternate needs a surviving onward route.                                                                                   |
| Network controls           | Per-device master/send/receive/directory preferences, physical-LAN-only discovery and direct LAN/Tailscale relay selection.                      | [Privacy controls](../docs/privacy-controls.md); visibility does not grant conversation authority or create a firewall.                                                                 |
| Files and folders          | Encrypted chunks, exact-offer consent, durable decisions, restart recovery, integrity checks and recipient completion.                           | [File flow](../docs/network-design-reference.md#e-files-folders-consent-and-completion); card arrival is not byte completion.                                                           |
| Linked devices             | Code-authorized enrollment, certified sibling synchronization and device-local category preferences.                                             | [Pairing and replay](../docs/network-design-reference.md#g-linking-and-ongoing-account-synchronization); full replay needs its own live authenticated route.                            |
| Calls                      | Optional device-addressed live Noise signaling and separate WebRTC media.                                                                        | No post-office signaling fallback or TURN service; native WebView and physical capture acceptance remain separate.                                                                      |
| Desktop presentation       | Shared person/relay classification, account/device profile details, themes, avatars, stickers, virtualized navigation and optional pack installation. | [Visual system](../frontend/DESIGN.md) · [Customization packs](../docs/CUSTOMIZATION_PACKS.md).                                                                                         |
| Local privacy and recovery | Privacy presets, lock controls, hidden contacts, local retention, recall and encrypted manual backup/restore.                                    | [Privacy](../docs/privacy-controls.md) · [Backup/recovery](../docs/backup-recovery.md); restore creates a new device and cannot revoke an old one.                                      |

## Deliberate design boundaries

- **Pairing authorization:** a one-time 128-bit code binds the linker and joiner
  device keys. Durable enrollment invalidates old sessions; interrupted adoption
  has a restricted code-authenticated retry. There is no separate SAS ceremony.
- **Relay metadata:** production relays store opaque outer events, not readable
  original authors, conversation IDs or channel controls. Connection identities,
  pseudonymous mailboxes, size buckets and timing remain observable. See
  [the exact privacy boundary](../docs/post-office-metadata-privacy.md).
- **Bounded custody:** relay copies have capacity limits and a 30-day maximum age;
  this is not guaranteed minimum retention or permanent storage.
- **Connections:** the client Node has bounded sequential session reuse, not one
  multiplexed socket per relay or an eight-socket ceiling for the whole machine.
- **Reachability and trust:** Tailscale does not merge LANs; explicit relay trust
  and client directory consent are independent of routing.
- **Membership presentation:** removed group members' past reactions no longer
  render under the current-membership visibility rule.
- **Linux dependency constraint:** the maintained
  [GLib compatibility workflow](../.github/workflows/glib-0.20-watch.yml) tracks the
  GTK/Tauri dependency gate. Consult the lockfile and security configuration before
  changing versions; do not treat this note as a vulnerability waiver.

## Evidence and future decisions

The [implementation/evidence tracker](../docs/network-design-reference.md#implementation-and-evidence-tracker)
records named logical and physical checks. Three independent physical LANs, a
separate ordinary client host on the mini's LAN, native macOS WebView media and
physical camera/microphone quality remain distinct acceptance cases.

New protocol capabilities such as true multiplexing, automatic federation trust,
mailbox-backed calling, TURN or stronger replicated-storage guarantees require
an explicit design and new evidence. They are not implied by the implemented
capabilities above.

## Shared project narrative

Explain the whole communication model in this order, regardless of which feature
changed most recently:

1. **Encrypted communication on a LAN:** local identities, signed discovery and
   authenticated direct connections; no internet or central messaging service is
   required for reachable LAN peers.
2. **Decentralized synchronization:** authorized peers exchange signed,
   content-addressed events. Multi-node synchronization is bounded by retained data
   and available paths, rather than dependent on one permanent sender.
3. **Other LANs and sites:** existing routed paths or opted-in, trusted post-office
   bridges/federation connect participants. Mesh-Talk does not provide a VPN, forward
   all LAN multicast or merge subnets.
4. **Offline delivery:** optional peer-operated post offices temporarily hold
   recipient-encrypted events, subject to capacity and a 30-day maximum age.
5. **Reconnection and group recovery:** authorized members with sharing enabled can
   supply retained messages and eligible file chunks, even without the original
   sender. A reachable source, receiving approval and retained content are required.
6. **Linked devices:** certified devices can synchronize selected account history,
   file cards and attachment contents over eligible direct device paths.

Use “no central server required” when describing serverless operation. Optional
post offices are services run by peers; serverless does not mean the project can
never use a server. Decentralized does not mean unrestricted routing, automatic
trust, infinite storage or guaranteed delivery. Encryption protects content; peers
and relays still observe some connection and routing metadata.

# Mesh-Talk domain language

Mesh-Talk supports private conversations between authenticated participants across
local and existing routed networks, with optional peer-operated encrypted custody.
This is the canonical glossary; [DDD conventions](docs/domain-design.md) own its
use in code, ownership decisions and documentation.

## Identity and access

**Local user**:
A local sign-in identity and its protected application data. A local user is not
the cross-device mesh account or a network device.
_Avoid_: account ID, device ID when referring to the local login identity.

**Username / account login name**:
The name entered at sign-in. Linked desktop devices use the kept account's same
login name and password. It is distinct from the account nickname and from the
immutable local storage username retained internally for an existing local user.
_Avoid_: account ID, device ID, nickname, storage directory as interchangeable names.

**Local storage username**:
The existing per-device storage namespace for a local user. Account login
migration preserves this name and the local-user UUID; a credential envelope maps
the shared login to the retained local owner and its separate storage secrets.
_Avoid_: account login name, account ID, shared password.

**Display name**:
A human-readable label for presentation. It is neither unique identity nor
proof of authority.
_Avoid_: identifier, verified identity.

**Account**:
A cryptographic identity shared across certified devices. Account identity does
not depend on a desktop login, IP address or display name.
_Avoid_: local user, machine, device.

**Account profile**:
Account-authenticated nickname, biography and avatar, saved through ordinary
profile editing and synchronized automatically. It carries read-only creation
metadata when known; revisions order updates across devices.
_Avoid_: local login profile, device identity, proof of a person's identity.

Linked devices share account login credentials through private account access. Login names remain distinct from public nicknames; device identities and local encrypted-storage secrets remain distinct.

**Device**:
A participant identified by its persistent signing and key-agreement identity.
Restarting a process does not by itself create a new device.
_Avoid_: running instance, account, physical computer.

**Device certificate**:
An account-signed binding of a device's public identity to that account.
_Avoid_: discovery record, membership grant.

**Account group role**:
The account's accepted member or owner role in a channel. Certified devices
present the same account role. The public membership state and verified account
bindings establish that role; device reachability determines execution
availability, not a different role. Legacy public controls retain their existing
signer requirements.
_Avoid_: online status, device approval, shared group reference.

**Account group operation**:
An account-authorized intent to change channel state or send channel content.
Its pending identity is distinct from the public events that commit its effects.
Execution may use an authorized device without changing the account's role or
reattributing existing public events.
_Avoid_: committed event before acceptance, device-specific permission.

**Peer**:
Another known network device, including an infrastructure device when the role
permits it. A peer is not necessarily a person or a channel member.
_Avoid_: user, contact, member as interchangeable names.

**Contact**:
An account represented in local conversation/contact state. Contact visibility
is separate from discovery, delivery permission and channel membership.
Automatic [never-chatted contact expiry](docs/privacy-controls.md#discovered-contacts-without-chat-history)
is a local presentation policy, distinct from personal conversation removal.
_Avoid_: online peer, accepted member.

**Desktop session**:
One authenticated local user's login lifetime. A subsequent login starts a new
lifetime even when it belongs to the same local user.
_Avoid_: transport session, ratchet session, account lifetime.

# Module Ownership and Reuse

This is the implementation ownership map for maintaining Mesh Talk and assigning
parallel work. Use it to locate the owner of a decision before adding another
implementation. Network semantics and configuration belong to the
[communication architecture](network-design-reference.md); this document defines
where those decisions live in code and how to change them safely.

The [canonical glossary](../CONTEXT.md) defines domain concepts;
[DDD conventions](domain-design.md) define modeling terms and identifier mappings.
The layers and owners below are implementation responsibilities, not declarations
that every module or crate is a separate DDD bounded context.

## 1. Dependency direction

| Layer                                       | Owns                                                                                          | Depends on                                              | Must delegate                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Protocol core: `crates/mesh-talk-core`      | Identity, membership, encryption, admission, persistence, transport and delivery correctness  | Rust libraries and its internal modules                 | Native platform behavior and presentation                            |
| Desktop host: `src-tauri`                   | Session/runtime installation, OS integration, settings persistence, authorized IPC adaptation | Core public exports                                     | Wire validation, cryptographic authority and delivery state machines |
| Typed IPC: `frontend/src/lib/api`           | Command names, payload shapes, typed results                                                  | Shared types, Tauri APIs and sibling adapters           | UI stores, React features and business decisions                     |
| Application stores: `frontend/src/store`    | Reactive state, owner-scoped work, optimistic intents, cache transitions                      | Typed adapters and shared projections                   | Core authority and feature rendering                                 |
| Feature modules: `frontend/src/features`    | User interaction and composition                                                              | Stores, typed adapters, shared models and UI primitives | Reimplementation of identity, policy or delivery rules               |
| UI primitives: `frontend/src/components/ui` | Accessible visual controls                                                                    | React/Radix and styling helpers                         | Session lifecycle and protocol policy                                |

The bot integration service in `crates/mesh-talk-integrations` depends on the core
and host-supplied admission ports. It owns grants, bounded metadata audit and
private IPC and its fixed-route loopback HTTP adapter; `crates/mesh-talk-mcp` owns SDK/stdio translation only. Core
`node/outgoing_message.rs` owns retry-safe event acceptance and sender-state WAL
recovery. Desktop `src-tauri/src/integrations.rs` binds exact-session leases and
graceful listener retirement. `integrations/local_access.rs` owns serialized
settings/startup control and the single desktop service handle;
`integrations/instructions.rs` owns only the marked user-level bootstrap file.
Both transports share one integration service/registry and core sending path.
`http.rs` owns public static discovery, request limits and fixed scoped routes;
request schemas derive from the existing models. The Agent access settings UI uses
the shared save coordinator and an explicit-owner typed adapter. See
[desktop local access](bot-integrations.md#desktop-local-agent-access).

The local access owner persists absolute authorization deadlines and preserves
them across service retries and session/runtime restarts. Only an explicitly
verified enable, duration extension or renewal can extend authority. The shared
integration grant authorizer checks expiry again at core acceptance. The desktop
activity view uses the existing registry's bounded content-free send projection:
read the live service registry while its supervisor exists, and open the saved
registry only after its writer has stopped under the same controller serialization.
The UI never creates a second grant-store owner or attributes a shared credential
to a particular AI application. See [authorization lifetime](bot-integrations.md#lifecycle-and-authority).

The headless CLI uses the core directly. A protocol change should not require
Tauri; a presentation change should not alter the wire protocol. Not every helper
in `lib/` is pure: `theme.ts`, for example, owns reactive appearance effects. Use
specific modules rather than assuming the directory name implies purity.

The existing API facade remains stable. Its settings owner resolver is composed
at the application seam; adapters never import stores. ESLint enforces that rule
for alias imports and relative imports at any nesting depth. The auth store uses
low-level adapters to avoid recreating the facade/settings/auth runtime cycle.

ESLint also rejects static imports of rendering modules (`components/` and
`features/`) from stores and IPC adapters, including type-only imports and nested
relative paths. Shared presence vocabulary lives in `lib…3380 tokens truncated…machine.
- **Reachability and trust:** Tailscale does not merge LANs; explicit relay trust
  and client directory consent are independent of routing.
- **Membership presentation:** removed group members' past reactions no longer
  render under the current-membership visibility rule.
- **Linux dependency constraint:** the maintained
  [GLib compatibility workflow](../.github/workflows/glib-0.20-watch.yml) tracks the
  GTK/Tauri dependency gate. Consult the lockfile and security configuration before
  changing versions; do not treat this note as a vulnerability waiver.

## Evidence and future decisions

The [implementation/evidence tracker](../docs/network-design-reference.md#implementation-and-evidence-tracker)
records named logical and physical checks. Three independent physical LANs, a
separate ordinary client host on the mini's LAN, native macOS WebView media and
physical camera/microphone quality remain distinct acceptance cases.

New protocol capabilities such as true multiplexing, automatic federation trust,
mailbox-backed calling, TURN or stronger replicated-storage guarantees require
an explicit design and new evidence. They are not implied by the implemented
capabilities above.
# Documentation guidelines

Mesh-Talk documentation should help a reader make a decision or complete a task.
Keep one coherent product story across surfaces, with details in the document that
owns them. A feature does not need a new paragraph everywhere it is mentioned.

## Audience and ownership

| Surface                                                      | Reader's question                                                     | Owns                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Project site](../site/index.html)                           | Is Mesh-Talk for me?                                                  | Product model, trust boundaries in plain language, representative UI, download and documentation paths.                                            |
| [Root README](../README.md)                                  | What is it, how do I start, and where is the source?                  | Concise orientation, supported communication paths, first run, repository map.                                                                     |
| [Documentation hub](README.md)                               | Which guide answers my question?                                      | Task-based routes and a complete catalog of maintained guides and evidence.                                                                        |
| [Architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md)                              | How does the system work?                                             | Protocol, modules, data flow, crypto, wire compatibility, and technical limits.                                                                    |
| [Network architecture baseline](network-design-reference.md) | Which communication model and contracts must future changes preserve? | Network design principles, module ownership, topology scenarios, policy interactions, resource budgets and feature-specific acceptance boundaries. |
| Feature and operations guides                                | How do I configure or use this capability?                            | Exact steps, options, examples, constraints, and troubleshooting for their topic.                                                                  |
| [Evaluation inputs](evals/README.md)                         | Which reusable cases and rubrics apply?                               | Maintained suites, inventory and prompts; generated evidence belongs in PR/CI artifacts.                                                           |

The site and README may summarize a capability, but link to its owning guide
for setup, flags, support matrices, and changing limits. Do not copy a CLI option
table, release procedure, or full feature inventory into either overview.

The [change alignment checklist](maintenance-checklist.md) owns the cross-surface
maintenance inventory: select applicable items when behavior changes, identify
generated and externally published consumers, and record evidence or follow-ups
in the PR. This guide owns writing and audience rules; the checklist links to
existing owners rather than duplicating their product contracts.

## Shared domain language

[CONTEXT.md](../CONTEXT.md) owns domain definitions; [DDD conventions](domain-design.md)
own modeling vocabulary, identifier mappings and the reference index. Use those
terms in guides, code comments and reviews. Keep technical invariants in the
architecture/network references and implementation ownership in the module map.
Do not create feature-local glossaries that redefine account/device identity,
conversation membership, lifecycle or delivery outcomes.

## Shared project narrative

Explain the whole communication model in this order, regardless of which feature
changed most recently:

1. **Encrypted communication on a LAN:** local identities, signed discovery and
   authenticated direct connections; no internet or central messaging service is
   required for reachable LAN peers.
2. **Decentralized synchronization:** authorized peers exchange signed,
   content-addressed events. Multi-node synchronization is bounded by retained data
   and available paths, rather than dependent on one permanent sender.
3. **Other LANs and sites:** existing routed paths or opted-in, trusted post-office
   bridges/federation connect participants. Mesh-Talk does not provide a VPN, forward
   all LAN multicast or merge subnets.
4. **Offline delivery:** optional peer-operated post offices temporarily hold
   recipient-encrypted events, subject to capacity and a 30-day maximum age.
5. **Reconnection and group recovery:** authorized members with sharing enabled can
   supply retained messages and eligible file chunks, even without the original
   sender. A reachable source, receiving approval and retained content are required.
6. **Linked devices:** certified devices can synchronize selected account history,
   file cards and attachment contents over eligible direct device paths.

Use “no central server required” when describing serverless operation. Optional
post offices are services run by peers; serverless does not mean the project can
never use a server. Decentralized does not mean unrestricted routing, automatic
trust, infinite storage or guaranteed delivery. Encryption protects content; peers
and relays still observe some connection and routing metadata.

# Mesh-Talk domain language

Mesh-Talk supports private conversations between authenticated participants across
local and existing routed networks, with optional peer-operated encrypted custody.
This is the canonical glossary; [DDD conventions](docs/domain-design.md) own its
use in code, ownership decisions and documentation.

## Identity and access

**Local user**:
A local sign-in identity and its protected application data. A local user is not
the cross-device mesh account or a network device.
_Avoid_: account ID, device ID when referring to the local login identity.

**Username / account login name**:
The name entered at sign-in. Linked desktop devices use the kept account's same
login name and password. It is distinct from the account nickname and from the
immutable local storage username retained internally for an existing local user.
_Avoid_: account ID, device ID, nickname, storage directory as interchangeable names.

**Local storage username**:
The existing per-device storage namespace for a local user. Account login
migration preserves this name and the local-user UUID; a credential envelope maps
the shared login to the retained local owner and its separate storage secrets.
_Avoid_: account login name, account ID, shared password.

**Display name**:
A human-readable label for presentation. It is neither unique identity nor
proof of authority.
_Avoid_: identifier, verified identity.

**Account**:
A cryptographic identity shared across certified devices. Account identity does
not depend on a desktop login, IP address or display name.
_Avoid_: local user, machine, device.

**Account profile**:
Account-authenticated nickname, biography and avatar, saved through ordinary
profile editing and synchronized automatically. It carries read-only creation
metadata when known; revisions order updates across devices.
_Avoid_: local login profile, device identity, proof of a person's identity.

Linked devices share account login credentials through private account access. Login names remain distinct from public nicknames; device identities and local encrypted-storage secrets remain distinct.

**Device**:
A participant identified by its persistent signing and key-agreement identity.
Restarting a process does not by itself create a new device.
_Avoid_: running instance, account, physical computer.

**Device certificate**:
An account-signed binding of a device's public identity to that account.
_Avoid_: discovery record, membership grant.

**Account group role**:
The account's accepted member or owner role in a channel. Certified devices
present the same account role. The public membership state and verified account
bindings establish that role; device reachability determines execution
availability, not a different role. Legacy public controls retain their existing
signer requirements.
_Avoid_: online status, device approval, shared group reference.

**Account group operation**:
An account-authorized intent to change channel state or send channel content.
Its pending identity is distinct from the public events that commit its effects.
Execution may use an authorized device without changing the account's role or
reattributing existing public events.
_Avoid_: committed event before acceptance, device-specific permission.

**Peer**:
Another known network device, including an infrastructure device when the role
permits it. A peer is not necessarily a person or a channel member.
_Avoid_: user, contact, member as interchangeable names.

**Contact**:
An account represented in local conversation/contact state. Contact visibility
is separate from discovery, delivery permission and channel membership.
Automatic [never-chatted contact expiry](docs/privacy-controls.md#discovered-contacts-without-chat-history)
is a local presentation policy, distinct from personal conversation removal.
_Avoid_: online peer, accepted member.

**Desktop session**:
One authenticated local user's login lifetime. A subsequent login starts a new
lifetime even when it belongs to the same local user.
_Avoid_: transport session, ratchet session, account lifetime.

# Implementation status and acceptance boundaries

This stable path is the current status index, not a chronological TODO list or a
claim that every topology/platform combination has been verified. Feature and
protocol details belong to the linked owning guides; Git history records completed
work.

## Current capability areas

| Area                       | Implemented behavior                                                                                                                                  | Reference / boundary                                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Direct conversations       | Signed discovery, identity-pinned Noise/TCP, encrypted account-addressed DMs, replies, reactions, mentions, search and retained history.              | [Architecture](../docs/ARCHITECTURE.md); discovery and TCP reachability remain separate.                                                                                                |
| Groups                     | Signed membership controls, sender-key encryption, bounded fanout and authorized member recovery with per-member sharing.                             | [Group flows and scenarios](../docs/network-design-reference.md#d-group-creation-distribution-and-member-recovery); a removed/nonmember device cannot acquire authority from discovery. |
| Relay networking           | Equal trusted post offices, shared public enrollment, opaque custody/federation, direct-first attempts, soft preference and alternatives.             | [Network baseline](../docs/network-design-reference.md); an alternate needs a surviving onward route.                                                                                   |
| Network controls           | Per-device master/send/receive/directory preferences, physical-LAN-only discovery and direct LAN/Tailscale relay selection.                           | [Privacy controls](../docs/privacy-controls.md); visibility does not grant conversation authority or create a firewall.                                                                 |
| Files and folders          | Encrypted chunks, exact-offer consent, durable decisions, restart recovery, integrity checks and recipient completion.                                | [File flow](../docs/network-design-reference.md#e-files-folders-consent-and-completion); card arrival is not byte completion.                                                           |
| Linked devices             | Code-authorized enrollment, certified sibling synchronization and device-local category preferences.                                                  | [Pairing and replay](../docs/network-design-reference.md#g-linking-and-ongoing-account-synchronization); full replay needs its own live authenticated route.                            |
| Calls                      | Optional device-addressed live Noise signaling and separate WebRTC media.                                                                             | No post-office signaling fallback or TURN service; native WebView and physical capture acceptance remain separate.                                                                      |
| Desktop presentation       | Shared person/relay classification, account/device profile details, themes, avatars, stickers, virtualized navigation and optional pack installation. | [Visual system](../frontend/DESIGN.md) · [Customization packs](../docs/CUSTOMIZATION_PACKS.md).                                                                                         |
| Local privacy and recovery | Privacy presets, lock controls, hidden contacts, local retention, recall and encrypted manual backup/restore.                                         | [Privacy](../docs/privacy-controls.md) · [Backup/recovery](../docs/backup-recovery.md); restore creates a new device and cannot revoke an old one.                                      |

## Deliberate design boundaries

- **Pairing authorization:** a one-time 128-bit code binds the linker and joiner
  device keys. Durable enrollment invalidates old sessions; interrupted adoption
  has a restricted code-authenticated retry. There is no separate SAS ceremony.
- **Relay metadata:** production relays store opaque outer events, not readable
  original authors, conversation IDs or channel controls. Connection identities,
  pseudonymous mailboxes, size buckets and timing remain observable. See
  [the exact privacy boundary](../docs/post-office-metadata-privacy.md).
- **Bounded custody:** relay copies have capacity limits and a 30-day maximum age;
  this is not guaranteed minimum retention or permanent storage.
- **Connections:** the client Node has bounded sequential session reuse, not one
  multiplexed socket per relay or an eight-socket ceiling for the whole machine.
- **Reachability and trust:** Tailscale does not merge LANs; explicit relay trust
  and client directory consent are independent of routing.
- **Membership presentation:** removed group members' past reactions no longer
  render under the current-membership visibility rule.
- **Linux dependency constraint:** the maintained
  [GLib compatibility workflow](../.github/workflows/glib-0.20-watch.yml) tracks the
  GTK/Tauri dependency gate. Consult the lockfile and security configuration before
  changing versions; do not treat this note as a vulnerability waiver.

## Foundation qualification status

The [current-IM foundation inventory](../docs/module-boundaries.md#current-im-foundation-inventory)
binds the capability areas above to source owners, actual callers, store categories,
representative assertion bodies and remaining unknowns at source
`5fe57c380b4b047ced19337b1233013d6d0ffcd7`. Its implemented/partial/scoped-missing/unknown
labels describe static inspection scope, not new passing tests or accepted runtime
measurements. The [roadmap](../docs/development-roadmap.md#task-claims-branches-and-integration)
remains the sole foundation claim tracker and acceptance order.

Current indexed participant storage, direct-account desktop enqueue and group
account-operation submission paths must be distinguished from retained standalone
log/device-send compatibility callers and explicit physical-channel enqueue adapters. Experimental Bluetooth and historical mobile-PWA work are not production
foundation acceptance. The bounded F01 inputs have local static-review acceptance;
F02 verification, F03 measurements and F04 contract qualification remain outstanding
before construction. F01 does not certify F10 or authorize later features.

## Evidence and future decisions

The [implementation/evidence tracker](../docs/network-design-reference.md#implementation-and-evidence-tracker)
records named logical and physical checks. Three independent physical LANs, a
separate ordinary client host on the mini's LAN, native macOS WebView media and
physical camera/microphone quality remain distinct acceptance cases.

New protocol capabilities such as true multiplexing, automatic federation trust,
mailbox-backed calling, TURN or stronger replicated-storage guarantees require
an explicit design and new evidence. They are not implied by the implemented
capabilities above.
